1.content: Share Go components and build optional native providers for QuickGUI. An extension can be an ordinary Go package that composes QuickGUI components, or a Go package backed by a separately built native library. Start with Go when the existing UI and platform APIs cover your feature. Add a native provider when you need an optional native dependency, as the terminal and updater packages do.
1.keywords: extension authoring plugin native provider purego manifest ABI ServiceApi RequireExtension OpenExtension npm

2.hierarchy: Authoring Extensions › Choose an extension type
2.content: What you are adding What you ship Core changes Components, themes, or application logic A Go module None A backend using an existing provider contract A Go package, manifest, and native artifacts Must match a registered provider A new native service or native node kind The same artifacts plus a core integration Required today The native extension API currently requires core integration. The core recognizes terminal and updater ; it does not accept arbitrary third-party provider names. The CLI also requires npm names of the form @quickgui/native-<name> . A manifest alone does not register a provider, and an unrelated npm scope is not accepted. The native walkthrough below is for a contribution or a matching QuickGUI fork. Ordinary Go packages can use your own module path and release cycle. An extension runs in the application's process. The Go application loads the core and selected providers through purego. Each provider owns its backend dependencies; the core keeps the renderer, layout engine, and native event loop. Go edits reuse these libraries, so consumers do not rebuild the native backend on every edit.

3.hierarchy: Authoring Extensions › Share a Go component
3.content: Create a module under your own repository path, depend on the Go SDK, and export component functions. This package needs neither a native manifest nor an npm package: Call notice.Notice(message, ui.Style{Padding: 16}) inside a component or children block. The accessor stays reactive, and the caller's style merges after the defaults. Component functions declare children without returning a node. Use ui.OnCleanup for resources owned by a mounted component; keep application-wide services outside component ownership. Publish the module using Go version tags, and document the SDK versions you support. Consumers add it with go get using your module path. Transitive imports of terminal or updater still opt the application into those native extensions, so keep optional integrations in separate packages or build-tagged files.

4.hierarchy: Authoring Extensions › Lay out a native extension
4.content: For the rest of this guide, echo is a proposed service provider added to a QuickGUI checkout. It is not included in the stock core . The paths below follow the existing updater extension: Add the crate to the workspace members. Build it as a cdylib ; avoid dependencies on quickgui , quickgui-host , WGPU, or Taffy. Share the small ABI definitions from the same core revision instead of linking another copy of the runtime. The updater's crate and entry point are working references. The examples use release 0.1.3 . Replace it everywhere with the core release you are targeting. Native descriptor versions must exactly match the core version; ABI version 1 alone does not imply compatibility across releases. The Go manifest and npm package versions must agree as well.

5.hierarchy: Authoring Extensions › Declare the Go dependency
5.content: Place this manifest beside the imported Go package's source , not just at the module root or in application configuration: Names start with a lowercase letter and contain at most 64 lowercase letters, digits, or hyphens. The library field is quickgui_ plus the name with hyphens replaced by underscores. Do not include lib or a file extension in that field. The manifest is limited to 16 KiB, and an application can require at most 32 providers. The Go package records the same name during initialization and exposes an explicit startup function: RequireExtension only records a requirement. Do not load libraries, open windows, or start workers in init . Call Open after native.Run reports readiness, and wait for its successful ready callback before calling session.Command("send", value, done) . Close the session on the UI goroutine when its owner is disposed. Callbacks run on that goroutine too. A public package will usually wrap the raw JSON event string and session commands in its own typed options, events, and methods. The CLI discovers manifests through go list -deps , using the same entry package, target, and build tags as compilation. Transitive imports count; excluded files do not. Both the manifest and the RequireExtension call are needed: one controls bundling, the other controls loading.

6.hierarchy: Authoring Extensions › Implement the native contract
6.content: Use src/extension_api.rs from your target core revision. Only C layouts, fixed-width fields, borrowed byte spans, function pointers, and opaque handles cross the boundary. Keep Rust strings, trait objects, and allocator ownership inside the library that created them. A service implements ServiceApi.invoke and ServiceApi.shutdown . The following descriptor fragment belongs after those functions; ECHO_EXTENSION is the new kind you add in the next section: The descriptor, strings, and table have static lifetimes. Copy and validate borrowed request bytes before invoke returns, then enqueue work and return immediately. Do not wait for network I/O, another worker, or native main-thread execution. Bound queue size, message size, active sessions, and any retained data. Catch recoverable Rust panics before they cross an extern "C" boundary. The Go session protocol is: Request Parameters Provider responsibility start The options JSON passed to OpenExtension Use the request ID as the session ID; reply and retain its event sink A command such as send {"session": 123, "value": "hello"} Find that session and settle this command's own reply stop {"session": 123} Stop accepting work for that session, cancel its resources, and reply shutdown function No parameters Cancel all sessions without blocking the UI thread ServiceSink.emit kind 0 carries one successful JSON reply, kind 1 a UTF-8 error, and kind 2 a JSON session event. Use a valid JSON value such as null for a successful command with no result. The current host accepts at most 64 KiB per emitted payload. Payload bytes are borrowed only during emit ; the host copies them into its existing event queue. The start sink stays alive after the start reply so it can deliver events. Command sinks are separate. Call each sink's release exactly once, including errors and rejected work, after its final callback. Closing a session must suppress later events and release workers; keeping a library loaded must not keep its sessions alive. Extension images remain loaded for process lifetime because callbacks may still reference their function pointers. Use the updater for a complete service implementation, including bounded scheduling and callback ownership. Use the terminal provider for a typed frame contract. A native visual backend returns changed data to a retained core adapter; it does not run a second renderer. Calling ui.NativeElement with an arbitrary tag does not register a new node kind.

7.hierarchy: Authoring Extensions › Register with the core
7.content: A new provider currently needs these changes in the same core build: Add a distinct extension kind and, if necessary, a typed function table in src/extension_api.rs . Reuse ServiceApi for request/event services. Extend src/extensions.rs to validate the provider's name, kind, table size, ABI, and exact release version before storing its table. Preserve duplicate-registration checks. For a service, add its name to service(name) and include it in shutdown_services() . The existing host router then handles extension/echo/<method> through crates/quickgui-host/src/extension_services.rs . For a new visual node, add a core adapter and protocol/tag handling as well. Preserve retained node identity, fine-grained invalidation, and component cleanup. Add the provider to your build, version-sync, packaging, and release validation scripts. The built-in --extension build option currently recognizes only terminal and updater . The application must load this modified core alongside the provider. Publishing a provider compiled for a new kind cannot make an older stock core understand it. For a reusable native capability, contribute the core integration or distribute a coordinated core/CLI fork with explicit compatibility requirements. Under the current CLI rules, publishing under your own npm scope also requires a manifest-validator change in that fork; @quickgui is the project's reserved namespace.

8.hierarchy: Authoring Extensions › Build and package artifacts
8.content: Use TypeScript scripts run with Bun to build native artifacts once. This example scripts/build-echo.ts stages the current host architecture from a QuickGUI checkout after adding the crate: Run bun scripts/build-echo.ts on each supported target host. This script does not cross-compile. macOS targets use .dylib , Linux .so , and Windows .dll ; target directories are darwin-arm64 , darwin-x64 , linux-arm64 , linux-x64 , windows-arm64 , and windows-x64 . Ship only the targets you actually build and validate. The native npm package contains artifacts and exposes its metadata for the resolver: Keep this package optional. The Go import determines whether it is needed; do not add it as a dependency of the core npm package. Publish independent provider packages rather than packages for every combination of enabled features. The current QuickGUI release pipeline publishes macOS prebuilts; adding other targets requires building, packaging, and testing those targets explicitly. If your provider needs helper executables or resources, declare their basenames in a manifest resources object keyed by darwin , linux , or windows . Each platform accepts up to 16 distinct files; the same platform list applies to both architectures. Put those files next to the library in every applicable target directory. The CLI copies them alongside the native libraries and marks plain resource executables as executable. Directory resources use .qgr bundles produced by the repository's packResources helper. It preserves executable modes and confined relative symlinks with entry and byte limits. These are internal packaging helpers, not a separately versioned authoring SDK. Sparkle's framework configuration and nested signing are currently handled specially by the CLI; a different macOS framework needs its own signing/resource integration.

9.content: For local development, build the matching core and provider, then use their absolute paths while assembling a consumer app. QUICKGUI_EXTENSION_DIR points directly to the selected target's artifact directory, not the parent lib directory: Create that consumer example with an import of go/echo before running the command. An explicit extension directory is authoritative and must contain every required extension and declared resource, including transitive requirements. Without an override, the CLI tries a matching installed npm package, checkout staging, then an exact-version download from the public npm registry. Registry tarballs require SHA-512 integrity; the resolver extracts only declared artifacts and verifies cached bytes. Private registries are not an automatic-download option today. Before shipping, verify these behaviors: An app without the import bundles no provider or optional backend dependencies. Adding and removing a transitive import changes a fresh bundle correctly. The bundled executable loads the provider through purego with the matching core. Missing files, names, ABI versions, release versions, and conflicting requirements produce errors. Starting, closing before startup finishes, repeated closing, cancellation, and application shutdown release every callback context and worker. Events stop after disposal. Background work never blocks the UI. Clean sessions sleep; queues, snapshots, caches, and resource payloads have limits. Follow the performance guide . bun pm pack includes every library and resource your manifest declares. Install the resulting archive into a separate consumer, build with native source staging unavailable, and exercise it on each supported OS and architecture. The repository's scripts/check-extensions.ts checks the built-in providers and their combinations. Extend it for a contributed provider or write an equivalent test for your fork. End users receive the packaged application; they do not install Bun, Cargo, npm packages, or a native toolchain to run it.

10.content: Add optional Sparkle-compatible updates to a Go application. The optional github.com/egoist/quickgui/go/updater package provides automatic application updates. Importing it includes @quickgui/native-updater ; apps without the import include neither that library nor Sparkle. Ordinary Go edits reuse the prebuilt native artifacts.
10.keywords: updater sparkle appcast ed25519 extension updates

11.content: Generate an Ed25519 key pair with Bun tooling: Keep the private .key outside version control and copy the contents of .pub into quickgui.toml : The CLI embeds the current version, identifier, target-specific feed URL, default preference, and public key in the Go executable. On macOS it also generates Sparkle's Info.plist settings and signs the nested Sparkle helpers with the app's identity. Secret keys are never embedded. Developer ID apps are supported; App Store and sandboxed builds must exclude the updater import using a Go build tag or platform file.

12.content: Start after native.Run reports readiness, outside components. Share the handle between settings, menus, and any update banner. An updater belongs to the application, so closing a window must not close it. Call updates.Check(done) from a Check for Updates menu item, updates.Install(done) from an available-update banner, and updates.SetAutomaticChecks(enabled, done) from settings. Callbacks always run on the Go UI goroutine. State() reads the latest cached event without calling native code or polling. Initialization and commands report errors through their completion callbacks. Options can override the feed URL and public key. Windows/Linux also allow current version and identifier overrides; Sparkle reads those from the app bundle, and its public key must match the embedded SUPublicEDKey . Development builds are disabled by default, including when using a release-built native library. Use AllowDevelopment: true only with a deliberately configured test feed and disposable app bundle.

13.content: Event.Status is idle , checking , available , downloading , installing , or disabled . Events include version, plain-text notes, progress byte counts, the automatic-check preference, and an optional error. An explicit check that finds no update reports Kind == "up-to-date" on the portable backend. macOS also uses Sparkle's standard result windows. On macOS, scheduled discoveries are retained for an in-app banner. Manual checks promote a retained result into Sparkle's standard UI. Sparkle owns download, verification, installation, scheduling, and relaunch. Its persisted preference takes precedence over the packaged default. Windows and Linux perform one quiet check per launch when enabled, and another when automatic checking is enabled. There is no idle polling timer. Download progress is throttled to at most ten events per second plus completion. Checks and installation cannot overlap; an explicit check adopts an in-flight automatic check. The portable installer verifies the artifact before preparing a handoff. QuitRequired means the helper has validated its inputs and is waiting for the current process to exit. Call native.App.Quit(false, nil) after dealing with unsaved work. If quit is cancelled, the helper times out after two minutes and leaves the current application intact. Closing an updater cancels checks and pre-handoff downloads; an accepted installer handoff is already owned by the helper.

14.content: Platform Update payload Installation macOS ZIP containing the signed .app Sparkle 2.9.4, embedded only with the extension Windows QuickGUI NSIS .exe installer A helper waits for app exit, runs the verified installer with /S and the current install directory, then relaunches Linux Type-2 .AppImage A helper waits for app exit, replaces the user-owned AppImage atomically, and restores the old image if replacement or startup fails Linux .deb , system binaries, unpacked AppDirs, and root-owned installations report disabled ; use their package manager. A new AppImage must retain the updater import so the SDK can acknowledge startup to the helper. Linux backups are deleted only after that acknowledgement and a short startup grace period. Windows installer failures are reported; rollback remains the installer's responsibility. The portable backend supports HTTPS Sparkle RSS appcasts, raw Ed25519 enclosure signatures, semantic-version ordering, target-specific feeds, and Windows minimum-system requirements. It skips deltas and unsupported channel/rollout constraints. It does not implement every Sparkle feature. Feed reads are limited to 1 MiB, downloads to 512 MiB, and presentation notes to 16 KiB. Signatures and declared lengths are checked again by the installer helper before installation. No unsigned fallback is available.

15.content: Place the private key in QUICKGUI_UPDATER_PRIVATE_KEY (or SPARKLE_PRIVATE_KEY ), using your CI secret store. Alternatively, updates.ed25519SecretKey points to a local key file. Keys use Sparkle's current base64-encoded 32-byte Ed25519 seed format and also work with Sparkle's sign_update tool. The CLI signs the finished platform artifact and writes appcast-<target>.xml . Upload the versioned artifact first, then replace the feed at its configured HTTPS URL. Feeds are per target, so architectures cannot accidentally install each other's binaries. The generated feed contains the current release; it does not generate Sparkle delta archives or staged rollouts. updates.manifest = true enables generation for every production build. macOS archives preserve framework symlinks and should contain the Developer ID signed, notarized app. Windows requires makensis ; sign the installer with the configured Authenticode identity. Linux requires appimagetool to produce an updateable AppImage. Public-key mismatches, missing signing keys, missing installers, and unsupported payloads fail the build. Existing Rust users can explicitly enable the legacy updater Cargo feature for the Minisign JSON UpdateClient . It is no longer a default feature or part of the Go native core. That legacy client and its CLI manifest path remain separate from this Sparkle-compatible extension; use updater.Start , not the removed native.Updater facade.

16.content: The builder stages the shared library plus Sparkle resources on macOS, or the installer helper on Windows/Linux. The CLI discovers the import transitively and fetches the exact-version extension package when necessary. End users need only the packaged application. The current npm release matrix ships macOS artifacts. Windows/Linux implementations can be built from source on their target hosts; publishing those prebuilt targets follows the framework's broader platform release support. See the runnable example and native extension contract . Sparkle configuration and appcast details are documented by Sparkle .

26.content: entry is the Go package to build. The configuration file is evaluated by the Bun CLI. It is not part of the running application. You can also use quickgui.toml with the same settings: The CLI checks quickgui.toml before quickgui.config.ts . quickgui dev --config configs/dev.toml or quickgui build --config configs/release.toml selects a file explicitly. Relative paths are resolved from the project directory, and dev reloads config edits. Quote version values, for example version = "0.1.0" , and put application fields before the [native] table.

27.content: Use github.com/egoist/quickgui/go/native for windows and platform services, github.com/egoist/quickgui/go/ui for UI, and github.com/egoist/quickgui/go/reactive for owners and contexts. @quickgui/cli is a development dependency. Pin the Go SDK and CLI to compatible release versions. To share your own components or build an optional native backend, see Authoring Extensions .

28.content: Use QuickGUI UI reactivity to render retained native UI. Go components create retained native nodes. Signals subscribe individual bindings to the state they read.
28.keywords: go signal component reactivity lifecycle router

29.content: Every component uses func() , including window roots, routes, conditional branches, and children blocks. It declares zero or more children without returning a node. Components run once when mounted. UI calls inside a children block attach to that block’s parent. Use normal Go if and for for static construction; use ui.Show or ui.For when a signal must change the child structure.

30.content: Pass an accessor for changing text or properties. Calling count() while constructing a string captures its current value; placing the call in func() string keeps it reactive. Event handlers batch writes automatically. Use ui.Batch for a group of writes elsewhere, and ui.CreateMemo for derived values. String and numeric signals can be children directly: ui.Text("Count: ", count) . The prefix stays retained while only the number updates. Numeric bindings use strconv ; they do not parse a format string. For a combined string property, use strconv.Itoa(count()) and concatenation inside an accessor.

31.content: WindowOptions.Component creates one reactive root per window. Closing the window disposes its nodes and effects. Register resource cleanup with ui.OnCleanup . For background work, ui.Async delivers its result back to the UI goroutine and cancels when its component is disposed.

32.content: Capture native.CurrentWindow() while the component is mounting, then use the captured window in callbacks. Do not look it up from an unrelated goroutine. Window events and native requests expose asynchronous callbacks.

33.content: Declare routes with ui.Route and ui.Layout . A layout mounts its matched child with ui.Outlet . Read parameters with ui.UseParams , or navigate with ui.UseRouter .

34.content: Lay out and style native nodes with familiar properties. Primitives accept ui.Style{} records, event options, and children directly. Compound parts accept the same records through ui.PartProps.Style .
34.keywords: style layout flexbox grid color hover

35.content: Multiple style records merge field by field in order. A later record only overrides fields it declares, including nested Hover , Active , and other interaction styles. Shared records are never mutated. Numeric lengths are logical pixels; strings also accept percentages. Zero is an explicit value; nil omits a field. Run bun run fmt to format long calls consistently.

36.content: The padding remains 20, the radius becomes 12, and the active state changes only the background color. Nested states follow the same merge rules.

37.content: Set Display: "flex" , choose a direction, then declare sizing and alignment. A scrolling flex child usually needs MinHeight: 0 or MinWidth: 0 so it can shrink.

38.content: Grid uses familiar track strings. Place children explicitly when auto-placement is not enough.

39.content: Typography inherits through the node tree. Colors accept hex, rgb() / rgba() , or packed RGBA values. Pass color and numeric accessors for reactive paint or size changes.

40.content: Add Transition to the base style to animate changes between paint states. See Transitions & Animation for hover effects, signal-driven changes, timing, and reduced motion. Use Hover: &ui.Style{...} , Active , Focus , Disabled , and Selected for interaction styles. ui.When merges its records while the condition is true and restores the earlier fields when it turns false. Only affected bindings update; children remain mounted.

41.hierarchy: Styling & Layout › Groups and named group hover
41.content: ui.Group(true) marks an unnamed hover group; ui.Group("card") names it. A descendant’s GroupHover: &ui.Style{...} follows its nearest ancestor group, including named groups. ui.GroupHoverNamed("card", ...) follows the nearest ancestor with that name, skipping intervening groups with other names. Hovering any part of the group, including its padding and descendants, activates its rules. A nested group becomes the target for unnamed rules; named rules can still follow an outer group. With no matching ancestor, the rule has no effect. Repeated group rules accumulate in declaration order; a node’s own Hover wins for overlapping properties. Use paint properties such as colors, opacity, outlines, and transforms. Hover updates are handled natively without rerunning components or changing layout. GroupActive: &ui.Style{...} and ui.GroupActiveNamed("card", ui.Style{...}) follow pressed groups. FocusWithin: &ui.Style{...} follows focus in the node or a descendant. These states accept paint styles and cannot set the cursor.

42.content: Animate native style changes and images with retained Go components. Animate changes to retained nodes with ui.Style{Transition: ...} . The native runtime advances the frames; your component does not rerun for every frame. Import ui from github.com/egoist/quickgui/go/ui .
42.keywords: transition animation easing duration hover opacity reduced motion gif webp

43.content: Put the transition on the base style so it applies when the pointer enters and leaves. The same declaration works with other paint states, including Active , Focus , Expanded , and DragOver .

44.content: Use a signal or ui.When to change the target. The card below keeps the same node and children while its color and opacity animate. Updating the target during a transition starts from its current visible value, including when reversing direction.

45.hierarchy: Transitions & Animation › Timing and frame rate
45.content: Use ui.TransitionDeclaration when several properties share one timing configuration. Import time for the duration in this example. The corresponding longhand fields can also be set directly in ui.Style{} : Field Usage TransitionProperty A comma-separated string or []string of supported property names. TransitionDuration Milliseconds as a number, a time.Duration , or a string such as "180ms" or "0.18s" . The host bounds durations to 0–10 seconds. TransitionEasing "linear" , "ease" , "ease-in" , "ease-out" , or "ease-in-out" . "ease" aliases the default "ease-in-out" ; these select QuickGUI curves. TransitionTimingFunction Alias for TransitionEasing . TransitionMaxFps Optional frame-rate cap. Omit it to follow display presentation; completion still occurs at the transition deadline. A node has one duration, easing, and frame-rate cap for all selected properties. Comma-separated shorthand entries collect property names; the last duration and easing apply to the entire list. Delays, cubic-bezier() , and independent timings per property are not supported. Explicit longhand fields override the shorthand. A duration alone, such as Transition: 180 * time.Millisecond , transitions background, border, and text colors. Select "all" explicitly to include all supported paint properties. Use Transition: "none" to remove the shorthand declaration.

46.content: Transition name Go style field background-color or background BackgroundColor or a solid Background border-color BorderColor border-width BorderWidth and edge widths border-radius BorderRadius and corner radii color Inherited Color opacity Subtree Opacity box-shadow BoxShadow transform Subtree Transform , including translation, scale, and rotation "all" means these properties. Gradient stops, width, height, padding, and other layout values do not interpolate through Transition . Unsupported transition property names are rejected. For a sliding switch thumb, use Transform: "translateX(20px)" and Transition: "transform 160ms ease-out" , then change the target to "translateX(0px)" when unchecked. This moves the painted subtree and its hit area without moving neighboring layout. Transforms interpolate their affine translation, scale, shear, and shortest rotation; TransformOrigin itself changes immediately. The Go UI API exposes paint transitions and animated images. CSS keyframes, timeline callbacks, and spring declarations are not Go style props.

47.hierarchy: Transitions & Animation › Mounting and reduced motion
47.content: A transition animates a change on an existing node; initial styles are applied directly. Keep the node mounted while changing its target. ui.Show removes its children when false and does not wait for an exit fade. Opacity zero alone keeps layout and input behavior. For dialogs, ui.DialogRootProps.EnterDuration and ExitDuration control transition completion and closing-content lifetime; OnOpenChangeComplete reports completion. Those durations do not create visual styles by themselves. See Dialog . Transitions respect the system's Reduce Motion preference. native.WindowOptions.ReduceMotion accepts a *bool for an explicit window policy; leave it nil to follow the system. Motion resolves to its target under Reduce Motion. Hidden or occluded windows pause local transitions, and completed transitions stop requesting frames.

48.content: Pass an animated GIF or WebP path to ui.Image . The native decoder retains the frames and the file's repeat policy; no Go timer or per-frame signal is needed. The path must resolve to an available file, or you can pass a data URL. Package file assets with the CLI's resources option. See Image and project configuration .

49.content: Choose between primitives and accessible compound components. QuickGUI combines unstyled primitives with accessible compound controls. Compose both through ordinary Go functions.
49.keywords: view text button tabs checkbox unstyled

50.content: Start with ui.View , ui.Text , ui.Button , and ui.Input . Options and text can be passed directly. A func() { ... } argument groups multiple children under the current parent.

51.content: Compound families expose parts such as ui.Tabs.Root , ui.Tabs.List , and ui.Tabs.Panel . The core handles roles, keyboard navigation, focus, and control state. Create a part inside its root’s children callback so its context exists.

52.content: A controlled value is an accessor; its callback stores the value accepted by the control. Use a default value to let the component own its state. Optional scalar values use pointers, while multiple selections use slices.

53.content: The reference covers forms, pickers, layout and data, overlays, menus, and routing. examples/components contains all 42 original gallery demos, including a 5,000-row table and lazy tree. The separate examples/swift-ui gallery demonstrates native SwiftUI hosting.

54.content: Use PartProps.Style for each part. It accepts a style record, a slice of records, or an accessor returning either. This lets selection and theme signals update existing parts without rebuilding children.

55.content: Build controlled fields, choices, and selection controls. Keep field values in signals and write accepted changes back from callbacks.
55.keywords: input field checkbox radio select events

56.content: ui.Input and ui.TextArea host native text editors. Bind ui.Value to an accessor and update it from event.Value in OnInput . OnSubmit handles Return in a single-line input.

57.content: Field.Root associates a label, control, description, and error. Set Required , Invalid , and ValidationMessage from application state. ValidationMode and ValidationDebounceTime configure when the core requests validation; your application owns the validation rule.

58.content: Checkboxes accept bool or ui.CheckedIndeterminate through ui.CheckedState . Radio groups keep one value; checkbox and toggle groups can keep several. Read-only controls remain distinct from disabled controls.

59.content: Declare picker options through PickerSourceProps.Items . Select uses a chosen value; Combobox combines text filtering and selection; Autocomplete accepts free-form input. Multiple pickers use Values and OnValuesChange .

60.content: Plain buttons accept ui.OnClick(func() { ... }) . Use ui.OnClickEvent when you need *native.Event . Compound callbacks use typed values and include the native event when relevant. Keep UI state updates on the UI goroutine; use ui.Async for background work.

61.content: Present in-window overlays and operating-system dialogs. Use a QuickGUI overlay for application-styled content, or a native dialog for platform file picking and alerts.
61.keywords: popover dialog overlay alert file picker

62.content: A popover composes a trigger, positioner, and popup. The side is a preference; the core resolves collisions. Read the result through ui.UsePopoverPlacement inside the root.

63.content: Create modal content under Dialog.Portal . Dialog.Title and Dialog.Description provide its accessible name and description. AlertDialog adds confirmation semantics. Controlled roots receive both the next open state and its reason.

64.content: ui.SystemPopover hosts its body in an operating-system popover. Specify its logical width and height, then declare ordinary QuickGUI children.

65.content: Native dialogs use asynchronous callbacks. Capture the parent window while rendering and pass it explicitly to the request. A canceled open panel returns Canceled: true .

66.content: Mount real SwiftUI controls inside a QuickGUI UI application. The ui.SwiftUI family embeds real macOS controls in a Go application. Ordinary QuickGUI components work without it.
66.keywords: swiftui host slider toggle picker native

67.content: Create controls inside ui.SwiftUI.Host . The host defines the native view boundary and can size itself from its content.

68.content: Available controls include Button, Slider, Toggle, ProgressView, Stepper, TextField, SecureField, Picker, SegmentedControl, DatePicker, ColorPicker, and Gauge. Their platform appearance comes from macOS.

69.content: Bind an accessor and store the value returned by the native callback. A SwiftUI control and a QuickGUI node can share the same signal. DatePicker uses Unix timestamps in milliseconds.

70.content: MatchContents: true sizes both axes intrinsically. Use ui.SwiftUIMatchContents{Vertical: true} for an intrinsic height with an application-defined width in PartProps.Style .

entry is the Go package to build. The configuration file is evaluated by the Bun CLI. It is not part of the running application. Event.Status is idle , checking , available , downloading , installing , or disabled . Events include version, plain-text notes, progress byte counts, the automatic-check preference, and an optional error. An explicit check that finds no update reports Kind == "up-to-date" on the portable backend. macOS also uses Sparkle's standard result windows. On macOS, scheduled discoveries are retained for an in-app banner. Manual checks promote a retained result into Sparkle's standard UI. Sparkle owns download, verification, installation, scheduling, and relaunch. Its persisted preference takes precedence over the packaged default. Windows and Linux perform one quiet check per launch when enabled, and another when automatic checking is enabled. There is no idle polling timer. Download progress is throttled to at most ten events per second plus completion. Checks and installation cannot overlap; an explicit check adopts an in-flight automatic check. The portable installer verifies the artifact before preparing a handoff. QuitRequired means the helper has validated its inputs and is waiting for the current process to exit. Call native.App.Quit(false, nil) after dealing with unsaved work. If quit is cancelled, the helper times out after two minutes and leaves the current application intact. Closing an updater cancels checks and pre-handoff downloads; an accepted installer handoff is already owned by the helper.

Every component uses func() , including window roots, routes, conditional branches, and children blocks. It declares zero or more children without returning a node. Components run once when mounted. UI calls inside a children block attach to that block’s parent. Use normal Go if and for for static construction; use ui.Show or ui.For when a signal must change the child structure.

For local development, build the matching core and provider, then use their absolute paths while assembling a consumer app. QUICKGUI_EXTENSION_DIR points directly to the selected target's artifact directory, not the parent lib directory: Create that consumer example with an import of go/echo before running the command. An explicit extension directory is authoritative and must contain every required extension and declared resource, including transitive requirements. Without an override, the CLI tries a matching installed npm package, checkout staging, then an exact-version download from the public npm registry. Registry tarballs require SHA-512 integrity; the resolver extracts only declared artifacts and verifies cached bytes. Private registries are not an automatic-download option today. Before shipping, verify these behaviors: An app without the import bundles no provider or optional backend dependencies. Adding and removing a transitive import changes a fresh bundle correctly. The bundled executable loads the provider through purego with the matching core. Missing files, names, ABI versions, release versions, and conflicting requirements produce errors. Starting, closing before startup finishes, repeated closing, cancellation, and application shutdown release every callback context and worker. Events stop after disposal. Background work never blocks the UI. Clean sessions sleep; queues, snapshots, caches, and resource payloads have limits. Follow the performance guide . bun pm pack includes every library and resource your manifest declares. Install the resulting archive into a separate consumer, build with native source staging unavailable, and exercise it on each supported OS and architecture. The repository's scripts/check-extensions.ts checks the built-in providers and their combinations. Extend it for a contributed provider or write an equivalent test for your fork. End users receive the packaged application; they do not install Bun, Cargo, npm packages, or a native toolchain to run it.

For the rest of this guide, echo is a proposed service provider added to a QuickGUI checkout. It is not included in the stock core . The examples use release 0.1.3 . Replace it everywhere with the core release you are targeting. Native descriptor versions must exactly match the core version; ABI version 1 alone does not imply compatibility across releases. The Go manifest and npm package versions must agree as well.

Pass an accessor for changing text or properties. Calling count() while constructing a string captures its current value; placing the call in func() string keeps it reactive. Event handlers batch writes automatically. Use ui.Batch for a group of writes elsewhere, and ui.CreateMemo for derived values. String and numeric signals can be children directly: ui.Text("Count: ", count) . The prefix stays retained while only the number updates. Numeric bindings use strconv ; they do not parse a format string. For a combined string property, use strconv.Itoa(count()) and concatenation inside an accessor.

Pass an animated GIF or WebP path to ui.Image . The native decoder retains the frames and the file's repeat policy; no Go timer or per-frame signal is needed. Place the private key in QUICKGUI_UPDATER_PRIVATE_KEY (or SPARKLE_PRIVATE_KEY ), using your CI secret store. Alternatively, updates.ed25519SecretKey points to a local key file. Keys use Sparkle's current base64-encoded 32-byte Ed25519 seed format and also work with Sparkle's sign_update tool. The CLI signs the finished platform artifact and writes appcast-<target>.xml . Upload the versioned artifact first, then replace the feed at its configured HTTPS URL. Feeds are per target, so architectures cannot accidentally install each other's binaries. The generated feed contains the current release; it does not generate Sparkle delta archives or staged rollouts. updates.manifest = true enables generation for every production build. macOS archives preserve framework symlinks and should contain the Developer ID signed, notarized app. Windows requires makensis ; sign the installer with the configured Authenticode identity. Linux requires appimagetool to produce an updateable AppImage. Public-key mismatches, missing signing keys, missing installers, and unsupported payloads fail the build. Existing Rust users can explicitly enable the legacy updater Cargo feature for the Minisign JSON UpdateClient . It is no longer a default feature or part of the Go native core. That legacy client and its CLI manifest path remain separate from this Sparkle-compatible extension; use updater.Start , not the removed native.Updater facade.

Place this manifest beside the imported Go package's source , not just at the module root or in application configuration: Names start with a lowercase letter and contain at most 64 lowercase letters, digits, or hyphens. The library field is quickgui_ plus the name with hyphens replaced by underscores. Do not include lib or a file extension in that field. The manifest is limited to 16 KiB, and an application can require at most 32 providers. The Go package records the same name during initialization and exposes an explicit startup function: RequireExtension only records a requirement. Do not load libraries, open windows, or start workers in init . Call Open after native.Run reports readiness, and wait for its successful ready callback before calling session.Command("send", value, done) . Close the session on the UI goroutine when its owner is disposed. Callbacks run on that goroutine too. A public package will usually wrap the raw JSON event string and session commands in its own typed options, events, and methods. The CLI discovers manifests through go list -deps , using the same entry package, target, and build tags as compilation. Transitive imports count; excluded files do not. Both the manifest and the RequireExtension call are needed: one controls bundling, the other controls loading.

Plain buttons accept ui.OnClick(func() { ... }) . Use ui.OnClickEvent when you need *native.Event . Compound callbacks use typed values and include the native event when relevant. Keep UI state updates on the UI goroutine; use ui.Async for background work.

Platform Update payload Installation macOS ZIP containing the signed .app Sparkle 2.9.4, embedded only with the extension Windows QuickGUI NSIS .exe installer A helper waits for app exit, runs the verified installer with /S and the current install directory, then relaunches Linux Type-2 .AppImage A helper waits for app exit, replaces the user-owned AppImage atomically, and restores the old image if replacement or startup fails Linux .deb , system binaries, unpacked AppDirs, and root-owned installations report disabled ; use their package manager. A new AppImage must retain the updater import so the SDK can acknowledge startup to the helper. Linux backups are deleted only after that acknowledgement and a short startup grace period. Windows installer failures are reported; rollback remains the installer's responsibility. The portable backend supports HTTPS Sparkle RSS appcasts, raw Ed25519 enclosure signatures, semantic-version ordering, target-specific feeds, and Windows minimum-system requirements. It skips deltas and unsupported channel/rollout constraints. It does not implement every Sparkle feature. Feed reads are limited to 1 MiB, downloads to 512 MiB, and presentation notes to 16 KiB. Signatures and declared lengths are checked again by the installer helper before installation. No unsigned fallback is available.

The following descriptor fragment belongs after those functions; ECHO_EXTENSION is the new kind you add in the next section: The descriptor, strings, and table have static lifetimes. Copy and validate borrowed request bytes before invoke returns, then enqueue work and return immediately. Do not wait for network I/O, another worker, or native main-thread execution. Bound queue size, message size, active sessions, and any retained data. Catch recoverable Rust panics before they cross an extern "C" boundary. The Go session protocol is: Request Parameters Provider responsibility start The options JSON passed to OpenExtension Use the request ID as the session ID; reply and retain its event sink A command such as send {"session": 123, "value": "hello"} Find that session and settle this command's own reply stop {"session": 123} Stop accepting work for that session, cancel its resources, and reply shutdown function No parameters Cancel all sessions without blocking the UI thread ServiceSink.emit kind 0 carries one successful JSON reply, kind 1 a UTF-8 error, and kind 2 a JSON session event. Use a valid JSON value such as null for a successful command with no result. The current host accepts at most 64 KiB per emitted payload. Payload bytes are borrowed only during emit ; the host copies them into its existing event queue. The start sink stays alive after the start reply so it can deliver events. Command sinks are separate. Call each sink's release exactly once, including errors and rejected work, after its final callback. Closing a session must suppress later events and release workers; keeping a library loaded must not keep its sessions alive. Extension images remain loaded for process lifetime because callbacks may still reference their function pointers.
